text: Now, what makes an agent useful?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, typically we want agents to have a minimum set of capabilities.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And often this includes things like the ability to read data that you own or have access to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This might be like your email, your documents, maybe a customer CRM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We want the agent to be able to do its own research.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this might include searching the web, maybe reading documentation or pulling issues from GitHub.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we usually want it to be able to use external tools, for example, MCP servers or APIs, maybe SaaS platforms.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And useful agents might do these things with a human in the loop, or they might be doing it autonomously in the background.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But the things that make agents useful also make them dangerous.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In fact, together, these three capabilities make what Simon Willison coined as a lethal trifecta.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is a combination of access to private data, like the on-call agent's ability to query the customer data warehouse and interact with the billing database,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Exposure to untrusted content, like reading user-submitted tickets or reports from other agents or externally documented processes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the ability to communicate externally, like reading and writing with third-party APIs or SaaS services.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now together, these capabilities throw the doors wide open for attackers.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now agents are designed to get the job done, and they'll use all the powers that they have to do it, sometimes with very serious consequences.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But here's the thing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These incidents happen because humans give agents way more access than they need.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Overprivileged agents can act freely on decisions that they make, even if they do have supervision.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, forcing a human-in-the-loop approval just kind of passes the access control on to a consent fatigue user.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, we've spent decades solving access management for humans, so shifting responsibility to the user just sort of moves the security problem up the chain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what should we do about the lethal trifecta?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do we address it without compromising the agent's usefulness?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, just removing one or more of these capabilities is going to cause the agent to be significantly less useful.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So how can we keep all three but still be safe about it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, instead of breaking the trifecta by removing capabilities, we really need to control the agent's access so the attack surface is minimized and the blast radius is contained, but the agent still has capability and autonomy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So how do we do that?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Well, some options for controlling access, among others, are things like using OAuth, maybe using a vendor MCP gateway, or containing execution in sandboxes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, OAuth binds access to a grant.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: At grant time, the user consents to all of the permissions that the agent could possibly use.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, consent is granted before any task exists, so if you give a broad grant, then you end up withstanding access.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your agent is over-permissioned for any single specific task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you narrow the grant and you don't give it very many permissions, then the agent just becomes less capable.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Either way, OAuth alone doesn't provide task scoped access control.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An enthusiastic agent can both read and write in the same run, even if you only want it to read on this specific task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An MCP gateway binds enforcement to a route.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You get things like observability and rate limits, and you also get one policy decision point at the MCP layer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Policy runs per request, and access is granted per user, but the agent's granted access outlives any single task because the gateway still holds standing credentials.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now a sandbox binds execution to a process.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This controls the blast radius.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But useful work has to reach outside the sandbox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And when it does so, you end up with standing access again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now we've also seen plenty of stories about agents breaking sandbox containment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Sandboxes bound what the processes can do, but they don't control what is authorized to act outside the sandbox itself.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, even if you combined all three of the solutions, the agent still doesn't receive a runtime credential that's downscoped to only one task.
